strengths: The paper identifies and clearly motivates an interesting failure mode in MOTR-style trackers: track queries suppress detection quality. The empirical comparison with and without track queries, including the AP drop for MOTR and the much smaller drop for SelfMOTR, provides a useful diagnostic perspective on detection-association conflict.

The proposed SelfMOTR design is simple and technically plausible: a detection-only pass produces internal 4D proposals, which are then consumed with track queries in the tracking pass. This is a coherent alternative to using external detector proposals and fits the declared Algorithms/General contribution type.

The ablation studies are relatively thorough for the core claim. The paper compares detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, external/frozen anchor proposals, and self proposals; the self-proposal variant improves the MOTR validation baseline substantially on DanceTrack, especially in AssA and IDF1.

Main DanceTrack test results are competitive among end-to-end trackers: SelfMOTR reaches 69.2 HOTA and the best reported end-to-end AssA/IDF1 in the table, supporting the claim that internally aligned proposals can help association.
The method is reasonably efficient despite the dual decoder pass, with reported speed decreasing from 24.8 FPS to 20.7 FPS, which is a modest overhead for the reported validation gains.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental. The method is close in spirit to proposal-augmented MOTR variants, especially MOTRv2-style detector proposals, and the main difference is generating proposals from a shared internal detection pass. This is useful but not a major conceptual leap unless supported by broader evidence.

The strongest results are concentrated on DanceTrack. On MOT17, SelfMOTR is weaker than several end-to-end baselines and even slightly below the listed MOTR baseline in HOTA and MOTA, which weakens the generality of the claim that the approach improves MOTR-style tracking.

The final performance story is somewhat mixed: the method is competitive with CO-MOT on DanceTrack but does not clearly surpass the best end-to-end methods overall, and it remains below non-end-to-end or graph-based trackers in several settings. The paper sometimes frames the result more strongly than the evidence warrants.

The ablation in Table 5 is cumulative and mixes the proposed self-proposal mechanism with HSV augmentation, CrowdHuman joint training, and denoising. While the self-proposal gain alone is reported, the relationship between these training additions and the final test numbers could be clearer.

The claim of being fully end-to-end is debatable. Proposal filtering by confidence threshold and a two-pass detection-then-tracking structure are internal to the network, but the pipeline still has a proposal selection stage whose differentiability and training/inference consistency are not fully discussed.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places: exact decoder-layer choices for final models, query counts, proposal limits, matching costs, loss weights beyond lambda_prop, and implementation details for the shallow proposal pass are not specified enough for confident reproduction.

The evaluation scope is limited to two MOT benchmarks and pedestrian/person tracking. There is no analysis on more diverse domains, crowded MOT20-like settings, failure cases, or robustness to missed proposals, despite the method relying directly on proposal quality.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and useful issue in MOTR-style trackers: detection quality can be suppressed when track queries are active. The analysis comparing AP with and without track queries is a clear diagnostic and motivates the proposed direction.

The proposed SelfMOTR design is simple and practical: a detection-only pass generates internal 4D anchor proposals that are then reused in the tracking pass. This is easy to understand and could be useful for researchers working on query-based MOT.

The ablations are reasonably broad. The paper compares detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, external/frozen anchor proposals, self proposals, confidence thresholds, decoder depth, and runtime. The runtime overhead is also reported, which is important for MOT.

On DanceTrack, the method gives a large improvement over the MOTR baseline and reaches competitive association/IDF1 among end-to-end trackers, suggesting that the proposal mechanism can improve association quality in at least one challenging setting.
weaknesses: The main scientific contribution is incremental and very close to prior proposal-augmented MOTR variants, especially MOTRv2-style methods. The core idea is essentially to run the same model in a detection-only mode and feed its boxes back as proposals; the paper does not convincingly establish this as a substantial conceptual advance over using detector proposals or auxiliary detection branches.

The headline empirical case is weak. On DanceTrack test, SelfMOTR is slightly below CO-MOT in HOTA and below MOTRv2 in HOTA/DetA/MOTA, with only small gains in AssA/IDF1. On MOT17 test, SelfMOTR is worse than the MOTR baseline in HOTA, DetA, and MOTA, and clearly worse than MOTRv3/CO-MOT. This undercuts the claim that the approach is a broadly effective improvement for end-to-end MOT.

The gains are confounded by training changes. The final DanceTrack validation result includes self proposals, HSV augmentation, joint CrowdHuman training, and denoising, but the main comparison does not cleanly isolate the proposed method under matched training recipes against strong baselines such as CO-MOT and MOTRv3. The self-proposal-only gain is shown mainly against MOTR, which is no longer a sufficiently strong baseline.

The paper repeatedly claims to be detector-free and fully end-to-end, but the method still relies on COCO-pretrained Deformable DETR initialization, CrowdHuman joint training, hard proposal thresholding, and a two-pass proposal selection mechanism. These may be reasonable design choices, but the claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

The MOT17 result is particularly concerning: the proposed method does not improve over MOTR overall, yet the discussion frames it as being in the detector-free range and emphasizes a small AssA gain. A method intended as a general MOTR improvement should not degrade the standard benchmark without deeper analysis.

Several important experimental details are missing or underdeveloped: no variance over runs, limited benchmark coverage, no code/reproducibility discussion, unclear fairness of using QIMv2 and added data across all baselines, and limited analysis of failure cases or sensitivity to proposal count/threshold beyond two threshold values.

The writing sometimes overstates conclusions. Phrases such as 'fully decoupling proposal generation from association,' 'detection-association conflict is practically removed,' and 'novel paradigm' are not well supported by the modest and mixed empirical evidence.

The presentation has minor but noticeable polish issues, including awkward wording, a very limited limitations section, and figures/tables that do not always make the comparison protocol clear. These issues are secondary, but they reinforce the impression that the paper is not yet mature enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important issue in MOTR-style end-to-end trackers: detection quality is suppressed when track queries are active. The empirical observation that MOTR AP rises from 60.0 to 66.3 when track queries are removed is compelling and motivates the method well.

SelfMOTR is a simple and practically attractive idea: use a detection-only pass from the same model to generate internal 4D self-proposals, then feed them into the tracking pass. This preserves the detector-free inference spirit better than methods relying on YOLOX or other external proposal sources.

The ablation study is strong for the central claim. The paper compares detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, external-style 4D anchor proposals, and self-proposals, and shows that self-proposals recover the benefits of proposal-based tracking without a separate frozen detector.

Results on DanceTrack are competitive with recent end-to-end trackers: SelfMOTR reaches 69.2 HOTA, 59.3 AssA, and 72.5 IDF1, slightly improving association and IDF1 over CO-MOT while remaining close in HOTA.
The runtime analysis is useful. The method incurs only a moderate FPS drop from 24.8 to 20.7 on an L40S because the encoder is shared and only the decoder is run twice.
The paper is generally well written, with a coherent narrative from diagnosis to method to ablation. The contribution is incremental but clean and relevant to current transformer-based MOT research.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than major. The method is close in spirit to proposal-based MOTR variants such as MOTRv2, with the main distinction being that proposals are generated by a shared detection-only pass rather than by an external detector. This is useful, but not a fundamentally new tracking formulation.

The strongest evidence is concentrated on DanceTrack. On MOT17, SelfMOTR obtains 57.5 HOTA, which is below MOTR as reported in the table and clearly below recent end-to-end methods such as CO-MOT and MOTRv3. This weakens the claim that the approach broadly improves MOTR-style tracking.

The final DanceTrack gains depend substantially on HSV augmentation and joint CrowdHuman training: self-proposals alone improve validation HOTA from 51.2 to 58.2, but the final 64.4 validation result includes additional training/data choices. The paper could separate method gains from data/augmentation gains more clearly in the main comparison.

The paper does not evaluate integration with stronger recent query-based trackers such as CO-MOT or MOTRv3, which the authors acknowledge. Since the method is proposed as a general way to reduce detection-association conflict, this missing experiment limits the strength of the impact claim.

The method is described as fully end-to-end and detector-free, but it still uses COCO-pretrained Deformable DETR initialization and joint CrowdHuman training. This is standard practice, but the wording should be more precise: the method is detector-free at inference and does not require an external detector, rather than being free of detection pretraining/data priors.

Some implementation details needed for reproducibility are thin, including exact decoder depth used in the proposal pass, proposal caps or padding behavior, matching details for unmatched proposals in the proposal loss, denoising configuration, and whether all comparisons use exactly matched training schedules and data.

The paper lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. Given the small margins against CO-MOT on DanceTrack test and mixed MOT17 behavior, variance analysis would help distinguish robust improvements from benchmark noise.

strengths: The paper addresses a real weakness of end-to-end MOTR-style trackers: interference between object discovery and propagated track queries. The proposed SelfMOTR design is simple and practically motivated: run an internal detection-only pass, turn confident boxes into proposal queries, and use them with track queries in the tracking pass.

The empirical ablations are a strong part of the submission. The authors compare several ways of injecting detection priors, show a large DanceTrack validation gain from self proposals over the MOTR baseline, and analyze proposal sources, confidence thresholds, data scaling, and runtime.

The method is competitive on several benchmarks. It achieves 69.2 HOTA on DanceTrack test, close to CO-MOT among end-to-end methods, and reports the best BFT HOTA among the compared methods. The additional MOT17 results are useful and candidly show where the method is weaker.

The Track-Attention Mass diagnostic is a thoughtful attempt to explain the detection-association conflict rather than only reporting benchmark numbers. Even if not fully causal, it provides useful evidence about decoder query behavior.
The paper is mostly clear and well organized, with a coherent motivation, method description, and appendix ablations.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is essentially an internal two-pass proposal generator for a MOTR variant, conceptually close to using detector priors or 4D anchors. The paper’s claim of being fully end-to-end/detector-free is somewhat softened by the fact that it explicitly performs a detection pass and relies on COCO initialization and, for DanceTrack, CrowdHuman joint training.

The main benchmark evidence is mixed. On DanceTrack, SelfMOTR is slightly below CO-MOT in HOTA and below MOTRv2 overall. On MOT17, it is clearly behind stronger end-to-end methods such as MOTRv3 and CO-MOT, and behind several non-end-to-end trackers. The AnimalTrack improvement over TransTrack is only 0.1 HOTA, so the “new best” claim is technically true only within a narrow end-to-end subset and is not very compelling.

Some comparisons are hard to interpret for fairness. The method includes QIMv2, query denoising, CrowdHuman training, HSV augmentation, and dataset-specific re-identification horizons, while not all baselines appear matched under the same training/data recipe. The ablations help, but stronger controlled comparisons against CO-MOT/MOTRv3 under identical backbones and training data would make the case more convincing.

The attention analysis is correlational. Track-Attention Mass and entropy are plausible diagnostics, but the paper does not establish that the observed attention distributions cause the performance improvements, nor does it test alternative explanations such as extra decoder computation, stronger detection supervision, or the additional proposal loss alone.

Several reproducibility details are under-specified or awkwardly presented: the project page is blank in the abstract, some loss weights and architectural details are not fully specified in the main text, and the exact number of detection queries/proposals and shallow decoder setting used for the reported runtime are not entirely clear.

The manuscript has presentation issues, including placeholder headers (“Abbreviated paper title”), some cramped tables, citation inconsistencies such as AnimalTrack being cited as [37] in the dataset description while the reference list indicates [47], and occasional over-strong wording relative to the evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies a real issue in end-to-end transformer MOT: detection quality can degrade when detection and propagated track queries are decoded jointly. The detection-only vs tracking inference analyses and the proposed Track Attention Mass diagnostic are useful lenses for studying this behavior.

SelfMOTR is conceptually simple: it reuses the model's own detection-only pass to form 4D proposal anchors before the tracking pass. The ablations indicate that explicit proposal anchors improve HOTA/AssA over a MOTR-style baseline on DanceTrack validation.

The paper evaluates on multiple tracking benchmarks and includes several ablations on proposal source, confidence threshold, data scaling, decoder depth, and detection-association conflict. The reported runtime overhead is modest relative to the baseline.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is close in spirit to MOTRv2/MOTRv3-style detection prior injection, except the detector is an internal extra pass rather than an external model. This is a reasonable engineering variant, but the paper overclaims it as a new default design principle for unified tracking.

The main empirical case is not convincing enough for acceptance. On DanceTrack test, SelfMOTR is slightly below CO-MOT in HOTA and below MOTRv2 despite using extra training ingredients; on MOT17 it underperforms several end-to-end methods; on AnimalTrack it is not best overall and is only marginally above TransTrack. The strongest claim is BFT, but comparisons there omit recent end-to-end competitors such as CO-MOT/MOTRv3.

Fairness of comparisons is unclear. The implementation uses QIMv2, query denoising, HSV augmentation, and CrowdHuman joint training, making it hard to isolate the proposed self-proposal mechanism from accumulated improvements. Several baselines are not re-run under the same recipe.

The ablation story is incomplete. The proposal mechanism gives a gain on validation, but the final numbers appear to depend strongly on data augmentation/pretraining and denoising; the denoising gain itself is tiny. The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases, proposal recall/precision, identity switches, duplicated proposals, or how sensitive the two-pass design is to Ndet, proposal count, decoder depth, and runtime settings.

The attention analysis is suggestive but not rigorous. Track Attention Mass is correlated with the proposed design, but the paper does not establish causality or show that the diagnostic predicts tracking failures across methods. Some interpretations, such as 'healthy' balanced attention regimes, are speculative.

Reproducibility and clarity need work. The project page is blank in the abstract, several equations/text extractions appear malformed, and important implementation details for exact reproduction are underspecified. The method is described as detector-free/end-to-end, but it effectively runs a supervised detection pass at every frame, so the terminology should be more carefully qualified.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated algorithmic modification to MOTR-style end-to-end tracking: generating detection proposals internally via a detection-only pass, then using them as spatial priors for the tracking pass. This directly targets a plausible detection-association interference problem without relying on an external detector.

The empirical results are strong on several challenging benchmarks. SelfMOTR is competitive with the best end-to-end trackers on DanceTrack, achieves the best reported end-to-end IDF1/AssA there, and obtains leading results on BFT. The gains over the MOTR baseline in the controlled DanceTrack validation ablations are substantial.

The paper includes useful diagnostic and ablation evidence. The comparison of detection with and without track queries, proposal-source ablation, threshold study, data-scaling study, and runtime measurement all help support the central claim that decoupled internal proposal generation improves tracking.

The method is appealingly practical: it preserves a largely self-contained transformer tracking pipeline, avoids a separate pretrained detector at inference, and incurs only a modest reported runtime overhead because the backbone/encoder are shared.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper situates itself well relative to MOTR, MOTRv2/MOTRv3, CO-MOT, and tracking-by-detection methods.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. The method is close in spirit to prior detector-prior approaches such as MOTRv2 and to CO-MOT’s observation about latent detection capacity; the main distinction is making the prior internal via an additional detection pass. This is valuable, but conceptually incremental.

The strongest headline claims are somewhat mixed across datasets. On DanceTrack, SelfMOTR is slightly below CO-MOT in HOTA and below several methods in DetA/MOTA; on MOT17 it is clearly behind recent end-to-end competitors such as MOTRv3 and CO-MOT. The paper acknowledges this, but it weakens the case for broad state-of-the-art impact.

Some improvements are confounded by implementation upgrades. The main setup uses QIMv2, query denoising, HSV augmentation, and CrowdHuman training, and the ablations show a large gain from data/augmentation. The paper would be stronger with tighter comparisons showing how much of the final test-set performance is due specifically to self proposals under identical modern baselines.

The attention-mass analysis is interesting but not fully causal. It supports an interpretation of query interference, yet the link between the proposed Track Attention Mass/entropy statistics and tracking failure modes remains partly speculative; more direct interventions or per-case visualizations would strengthen this argument.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places. Important choices such as the final number of decoder layers used for proposal generation, exact Ndet/proposal caps, filtering/NMS details if any, and full inference protocol are not fully specified. The empty project-page field and placeholder running title also suggest the submission needs polishing.

The two-pass decoder design complicates the claim of a compact end-to-end tracker. Although no external detector is used, the method still effectively separates detection and tracking at inference, and the runtime/memory analysis is limited to a single hardware setting.
